row.title: Is it doing my thinking?
row.character_cast: Orbit opens, DiGi closes on where to stand
row.evidence_anchor: Bastani et al, PNAS 2025: unguarded AI cost 17 percent on the unaided exam, hints only avoided that loss with no gain over no AI at all
statutory_hooks: RSHE 2026 (media literacy and critical evaluation of online content)
JCQ Access Arrangements 2025/2026 (computer reader and human reader in reading assessments)
row.single_action_outcome: I can decide which part of a task has to stay with me.

slides.body: Not whether you use it. Where you let it in.
slides.title: Is it doing my thinking?
slides.script: Read the title, then the line under it, then stop. Do not open with a warning and do not open with a survey of who uses it. The whole lesson turns on the second line: nobody in this room is being asked to give anything up.

lines: Help that gets you to the work, or help that does the work. How do you tell them apart?
That is today, and it changes how you use every tool you have.
slides.script: Let Orbit land and say the lines. Then read the question on the wall once, in your own voice, and leave it hanging. Do not answer it. The next slide says what today is for, and the class talks before anyone is told.
slides.heading: Orbit

slides.why: You are going to be using these tools for the rest of your life. Nobody has taught you where to put them.
gains: A test you can run on any task in about ten seconds
A way to find out whether you actually learned it
The reason your brain feels certain when it is wrong
slides.script: Land the outcome as a decision, not a rule. They are not being told what to do with AI. They are being handed the thing that lets them decide, task by task, which is a bigger offer and they will notice.
slides.outcome: I can decide, for one piece of work, which part I have to do myself.

slides.prompt: Hundreds of pupils a bit older than you were asked to write a paragraph about AI, and they were told they could use an AI tool to help if they wanted. Guess: how many out of every ten chose not to use it?
slides.script: Take guesses before you say the number. Then tell them: 72 percent chose not to use it. Let that sit. Most of them have spent two years being talked to as though they are the one child in ten who hands in work they did not write. Say plainly that this lesson is not about that child. The study is Oxford University Press, June 2026: 704 pupils across 20 schools, and of those offered an AI tool for the task, 72 percent left it alone. Two honest limits if a pupil pushes: the task was a paragraph about AI itself, inside a study, which probably pushes the number up, so treat seven in ten as the ceiling rather than the everyday rate.
slides.lookFor: Guesses are almost always low, usually two or three. The real answer is about seven.

words.definition: To hand a job to something outside your head. A calculator, a note, a friend, a chatbot. Offloading is not cheating. Everybody does it every day.
Smooth and easy. Watch this one. Work that feels smooth while you do it is often the work you remember least.
When how sure you feel matches how right you actually are. Today you find out whether yours is.

slides.script: Offload is the load bearing word and it must land as neutral. If offloading were bad, writing anything down would be bad. Fluent is the trap being named early so it pays off in cycle three.
slides.heading: Three words for today

slides.body: Nearly a thousand secondary pupils, aged about 14 to 17, had their maths classes split into three groups. One group had no AI. One had a normal chatbot. One had a chatbot told to give hints and never the answer. Then the tool was taken away and everyone sat the same exam.
slides.script: Set it up as an experiment and hold the result back. Do not say what happened. The next two slides are the payoff and they only work if nobody has been told yet. If a pupil asks where: one large secondary school in Turkey, autumn 2023. Nobody in that study was as young as this class, so we are borrowing a result from older pupils, and saying so out loud is the same habit the lesson is teaching.
slides.heading: The help that costs you something

slides.script: Make them commit before you show them anything. Hands up for each. Guessing first is not a warm up, it is the thing that makes the answer stick, and it is worth telling them that.

options.text: The group who had the normal chatbot
options.feedback: Yes, and they had done best in every practice session. On the exam they came 17 percent BELOW the group who never had it at all.

options.text: The group told to give hints and never answers
options.feedback: They finished level with the group who never had AI. No penalty, and no bonus either. The hints did not make them learn more, they stopped them learning less.

options.text: The group with no AI at all
options.feedback: They are the line the other two are measured against. One group fell below them, one group matched them, and nobody beat them.

slides.question: Before you see the result. On the exam, with the tool taken away from everyone, which group came out WORST?

steps.text: Practice scores went up 48 percent. On the exam, with the tool gone, they scored 17 percent BELOW the group who never had it.
steps.title: Chatbot giving answers

steps.text: Practice scores went up 127 percent. On the exam they came out level with the group who never had it. Not ahead of them. Level.
steps.title: Chatbot giving hints only

steps.text: One instruction was different. Give a hint, never the answer. That was the only change.
steps.title: Same model, same school

slides.script: Give them ten seconds on the two numbers before you speak. The 127 is the one that surprises. The careful arm did not get a smaller boost for being careful, it got a much bigger one, and then it walked away with no damage. Say the limit out loud too: it did not beat the no AI group, it matched them. Guardrails stopped a loss, they did not buy a gain. Also worth knowing that both practice numbers were scored while they still had the tool in front of them, so they measure performance, not learning. Bastani and colleagues, PNAS, 2025.
slides.caption: What happened while they had it, and what happened when it went.
slides.heading: Same tool, opposite result
verdicts: The tool was not the problem
Where the effort went was the problem

slides.body: Your memory is not a bucket you pour things into. It is more like a muscle: it changes when it has to work. The moment you are stuck and reaching for something is the moment it changes. Skip that moment and the answer still arrives, it just arrives in your book instead of in you.
slides.script: Keep the muscle line simple and do not oversell the brain science. The honest version is that effort at the moment of retrieval is what makes memory stick, and that finding is decades old and solid. It does not need a brain scan.
slides.heading: Why the easy version teaches you less

slides.prompt: Think of one thing you are genuinely good at. Who did the hard part while you were learning it?
slides.script: Sixty seconds, take three. This is the cycle one landing and they should say the sentence rather than hear it. Football, an instrument, a game, cooking. Nobody names a skill they got by watching.
slides.lookFor: They say it themselves. Nobody gets good at something by watching someone else do it.

slides.body: Here is the thing that decides it, and it is not a rule about AI. Every task is trying to teach you one thing. Find that thing, and let the tool touch everything except it.
slides.script: This is the centre of the lesson. Say it slowly, twice. Note the shape: it is a question they answer per task, not an instruction they obey. That is deliberate and it is why it survives outside this room.
slides.heading: What is this task teaching you?

steps.text: A computer reader IS allowed. A flat machine voice says the words and hands you nothing else.
steps.title: GCSE English, the reading section

steps.text: A human reader is NOT allowed. A person reading aloud adds emphasis and meaning, and working out the meaning is what that section marks.
steps.title: Same paper, same section, a person reading

steps.text: What flips it is not the person and not the technology. It is whether the help hands over the thing being tested.
steps.title: Same pupil, same words out loud, opposite answer

slides.script: This is the one that makes the lesson fair, and it is worth getting exactly right because a teacher may repeat it to a SENCO. A computer reader is permitted, including in a paper testing reading: JCQ allows it by name. What is barred in a section testing reading is a HUMAN reader, because a person reading aloud supplies nuance, and the nuance is the thing being marked. A candidate who would normally have a reader gets up to 50 percent extra time in that section instead. Note it is sections, not whole papers: a human reader is fine in the writing section of the same exam. So say it plainly: a reader is not cheating and never was. Anyone in this room with an access arrangement is using a ramp and the rules agree with them.
slides.caption: Two real rules, same paper, same pupil.
slides.heading: The exam board already decided this
verdicts: A ramp gets you to the work

slides.script: Quick one. Most rooms get this. It is here to build the habit of asking the question before the harder case lands.

options.text: Swap. Turning French into English is the thing being tested
options.feedback: Right. The task is teaching you to hold those words. Handing that over leaves nothing behind.

options.text: Ramp. It is only a word list, the real work is memorising it
options.feedback: The memorising starts the moment you work out what the word means. Get the meaning handed to you and you have skipped the first pass.

options.text: Neither. It depends how many words there are
options.feedback: The number does not change what is being taught. A hundred words or five, it is the same skill.

slides.question: French vocabulary test on Friday. You ask a chatbot to translate the word list for you. Ramp or swap?

slides.script: This one splits a class and it should. Let them argue for a minute. The point is not the right answer, it is that they cannot get there without knowing what the task is for, which is the whole tool doing its job.

options.text: Ramp, if the write up is marked on your method and results
options.feedback: Yes, and notice it took reading the mark scheme to answer. A blank page is not the thing being taught. If you were being marked on writing an opening, the answer flips.

options.text: Swap. Any words it writes are its words, not yours
options.feedback: That is a fair instinct and it is the safer habit, but it goes further than the rules do. A sentence that gets you moving is a ramp when the writing is not what is being measured.

options.text: Ramp. Getting started is always the hardest part
options.feedback: Hard does not mean it is not the lesson. Sometimes the hard part IS the lesson. The question is what is being marked.

slides.question: Science write up on a practical you did. You cannot get the introduction started, so you ask for a first sentence. Ramp or swap?

slides.prompt: Name a task where the hard part is in the way rather than the point. Then name one where the hard part IS the point.
slides.script: Sixty seconds. Take one of each. If a pupil offers their own access arrangement as an example, take it warmly and move on without making it a moment.
slides.lookFor: Reading a long question in a maths problem. Handwriting neatly in a history essay. Against: working out the maths, choosing the argument.

slides.body: Here is the part nobody warns you about. When a tool explains something to you, it does not just do the work. It leaves you feeling like you could have done it yourself. The feeling of understanding arrives whether or not the understanding does.
slides.script: Slow down here. This is the most useful idea in the lesson and the one they have never been told. It is not a warning about AI, it is a fact about the feeling in their own head, which is far more interesting to a Year 8.
slides.heading: Close the tab and find out

slides.claim: Of the UK teenagers who said they were confident they could spot AI generated content, a quarter could not identify the AI image when they were actually tested.
slides.script: Fifty two percent said they were confident. A quarter of those confident ones got the image wrong. It was one image rather than a test with a pass mark, so say got it wrong rather than failed. Ask the room: did those people know they were about to get it wrong? No. That is the whole point. Being wrong feels exactly like being right. One thing to avoid: Ofcom's base here is teenagers, 13 to 17, so do not say children your age to a Year 7 class. Say people a bit older than you, and the point still lands.
slides.source: Ofcom, Children and Parents: Media Use and Attitudes Report 2025/26, 21 May 2026

slides.body: Pick something you learned this week that works in steps. Score out of 5 how well you could explain it. Now say it out loud, every step, as if to a Year 5. Score yourself again.
slides.script: Run it live, right now, sixty seconds, out loud in pairs. The works in steps part matters and is worth enforcing: this effect is strong for things with a mechanism and weak or absent for facts, dates and definitions, so steer anyone who picks one of those. Then ask for a show of hands: whose second number was lower? Many hands go up, not all, and a pupil whose score held is not a failed demonstration. Tell them the drop is not them being thick, it is the test working, and it is the only way to find out before a test does it for you.
slides.heading: The explain it back test

slides.script: Option two is the one to head off hardest. Nobody got worse. They got accurate. Say that phrase and leave it up.

options.text: You found the bit you had borrowed instead of learned
options.feedback: Yes. And you found it on a Tuesday for free, instead of in an exam hall. The gap was always there. Now you can see it.

options.text: You are worse at this than you thought
options.feedback: You are exactly as good as you were a minute ago. The only thing that changed is that you now know where the edge is.

options.text: You explained it badly
options.feedback: Sometimes. But explaining is how you find the hole, so a bad explanation has just done you a favour.

slides.question: Your second score was lower than your first. What does that actually tell you?

slides.prompt: If the feeling of understanding turns up whether or not you understand, what could you actually trust instead?
slides.script: They will get there. The answer is always some version of try one and see. Write the best version on the board in their words and keep it for the recap.
slides.lookFor: Doing one on your own. Explaining it. Tomorrow, with it shut. Anything that is an attempt rather than a feeling.

config.prompt: Two breaths with Orbit: in as Orbit grows, out as Orbit shrinks. Then tell your neighbour one thing from today that surprised you, and write it on your sheet.
config.heading: Half time

slides.script: Half time. Two breaths with the whole room, in as Orbit grows and out as Orbit shrinks. Then thirty seconds in pairs on one thing that surprised them, and they write it on their sheet. Nothing is marked and nobody reads theirs out. Then straight into the practise.

config.label: Ramp or swap . tap the class verdict

posts.why: Reading is in the way. The task is understanding the source, and that part is still all yours. The exam board permits a computer reader by name.
posts.text: You are dyslexic. You have a computer read the history source aloud so you can answer questions about what it says.

posts.why: Solving is the whole task. Nothing is left for you once the working is handed over.
posts.text: Maths homework on solving equations. You photograph each question and copy the worked answers.

posts.why: It marked, you wrote. The thinking stayed with you and you got feedback you would otherwise wait a week for.
posts.text: You have written an essay. You ask a chatbot to tell you which paragraph is weakest and why, then you rewrite it.

posts.why: If it is a Spanish writing task, that is a swap. If it is a geography project that happens to be in Spanish, it is a ramp. Check what is being marked.
posts.text: Spanish homework. You write it in English and have it translated.

posts.why: This is the arm of the trial that came out unharmed. Stuck for ten minutes is not noble, it is just stuck. A hint puts you back in the work.
posts.text: You are stuck on question four and have been for ten minutes. You ask for a hint, not the answer, then carry on.

posts.why: Reading the book was the task. You can produce something that reads well and know nothing, which is exactly the gap this lesson is about.
posts.text: Book review on a novel you did not read. You ask for a summary and write from that.

config.doneBody: Same six on the sheet now. This time your verdict needs the reason written next to it.

slides.script: Do case one first and do it deliberately. A reader is a ramp and the exam board says so. That settles the room for anyone in it who uses one. Case four is the one to spend time on: the answer genuinely is it depends, and being able to say why is the skill.
slides.caption: Sort the six together before the sheet.

slides.body: Take a real piece of homework you have this week. Write down the one thing it is teaching you. Then write one place AI may help, and one place it must not.
slides.script: This is the transfer and it is the part that leaves the room with them. Circulate. If a pupil cannot name what the task is teaching, that is worth knowing and it is often the more useful conversation.
slides.heading: Now on your own work

slides.prompt: Swap sheets. Do you agree with where your partner drew the line? Argue it out.
slides.script: Two minutes. The disagreements are more useful than the agreements and you want a couple of them read out.
slides.lookFor: Disagreement is the point. Ask them which of them had read the mark scheme.

slides.script: This is the fading rule and it is the answer to do I just stop. Ask for one step less than last time. Put it on the board.

options.text: Ask for one step less than last time
options.feedback: That is the whole method. Not stopping, not going cold turkey. One step less, once you have earned it twice.

options.text: Stop using it now you can do some of it
options.feedback: Too fast. There is real evidence that pulling support away too early leaves people worse off than keeping it. Drop one rung, not the ladder.

options.text: Keep going the same way, it is working
options.feedback: It was working. The help that fits you today is too much help next week, and that is a sign you improved.

slides.question: You have been using hints and you can now do the first three steps alone. What changes next time?

slides.script: Straight recall of the tool. If this one is shaky the lesson did not land and cycle two is where to go back to.

options.text: What is this task actually teaching me?
options.feedback: That is it. Everything else in this lesson hangs off that question.

options.text: Am I allowed to use it?
options.feedback: Worth knowing, but it is a different question. Plenty of allowed things still do your learning for you.

options.text: Would I be embarrassed if my teacher saw?
options.feedback: A decent gut check, and not enough. Embarrassment tracks the rules, not what you are losing.

slides.question: One test decides whether a tool is a ramp or a swap. Which is it?

slides.script: This is the one worth getting right. Everything they do afterwards depends on not trusting the feeling of having understood.

options.text: Almost nothing. Understanding feels the same whether or not it stuck
options.feedback: Exactly. That feeling is the least reliable thing in the room, which is why the explain it back test exists.

options.text: Quite a lot. If it made sense, you understood it
options.feedback: It made sense while it was in front of you. The question is what is there tomorrow with the tab shut.

options.text: It depends how hard the topic was
options.feedback: The feeling shows up on hard topics and easy ones alike. Difficulty does not make it more trustworthy.

slides.question: You read an explanation and it made complete sense. How much does that tell you about whether you have learned it?

points: Ask what the task is teaching you, then let it touch everything except that.
The feeling of understanding turns up whether or not the understanding did. Explain it back and find out.
Ask for one step less than last time.
slides.script: Read them. Do not add to them. Three is what fits in a head on the way to the next lesson.
slides.heading: Three things to take out of here

lines: Ask what the task is teaching you. Ask if the hard part is the teaching part.
If it is in the way, use the tool and say that you used it.
slides.script: The handover. Say nothing over it. When the last line lands, ask them to look at you and say the mission once more in your own words. DiGi closes on the next slide.
slides.heading: Your mission, on your next piece of homework

config.after: When the page is full, the big check earns Orbit's stamp.
config.prompt: Today filled part of the Making choices page. Tap to fill it in.
config.heading: The passport

slides.script: Thirty seconds, not a lecture. The passport is the record of getting ready for full access at sixteen, kept at home in the parents app, and every lesson here fills part of a page. Tap Fill the page, or hand the clicker to someone. Point at the area today built and the count moving. Say: when the page is full, the big check earns Orbit's stamp, and nobody can fail it. The parent note carries the home code that puts today in their own passport. The count on the wall is this screen's memory of your classes, not anyone's record.

lines: Nobody in here is being told to stop using it.
You are being told where to stand while you do.
The pupils who kept what they learned used it more than anyone. They just never asked it for the answer.
slides.script: Close on the third line and stop. It is the ban neutral position in one sentence and it is the thing they will repeat to someone else. Do not add a warning after it.
slides.heading: One last thing

dsl_note.note: This lesson is about learning rather than safeguarding, and carries no disclosure prompt. One inclusion point matters and is written into the script: access arrangements such as a reader, a scribe or text to speech are named explicitly as legitimate, because a lesson about doing your own thinking can otherwise be heard by a pupil with an access arrangement as an accusation. Staff should not apply the content as a blanket no tools rule, which would cut across the school's anticipatory duty under the Equality Act 2010 and the SEND Code of Practice.

parent_note.taught: Today we looked at where AI belongs in a piece of schoolwork. Not whether to use it, but which part of the thinking has to stay with your child. We used a real trial of nearly a thousand pupils a few school years older than yours where the same chatbot improved practice scores and then lowered exam scores, and the only difference was whether it gave hints or answers. Nobody was told to stop using anything.
parent_note.headline: What we taught today, and one thing to try at home
parent_note.passport: This lesson filled part of your teenager's passport page. The passport is the readiness record home and school build on the road to sixteen: skills proven at school, trust earned at home, each stage stamped when it is ready rather than when a birthday arrives. The skill proven today is deciding which part of a piece of work has to stay with them.
parent_note.try_this: Do not ask whether they understood their homework. Ask them to shut the tab and explain it to you, every step, as if you knew nothing. The place they go quiet is the part that was borrowed rather than learned, and finding it at the kitchen table is a great deal cheaper than finding it in an exam.
parent_note.family_question: What was tonight's homework actually teaching you, and where did you let it help? The first answer decides the second.

send.eal: The thinking test translates cleanly and is worth having in first language on the desk. Note that case four is specifically about working across two languages and is a good entry point for EAL pupils to lead.
send.sensory: The sort runs on paper if the board version is too busy. No sound is required at any point in this lesson.
send.attention: The thinking test is three questions and one decision at a time. Case cards can be handled one at a time rather than as a set of six.
send.communication: Every practise case carries a sentence stem on the sheet. The explain it back test may be done to a partner, to an adult, or written, and nobody is required to speak in front of the room.

keywords.definition: To hand a job to something outside your head, such as a calculator, a note or a chatbot. Offloading is normal and often sensible. The question is only ever which job.
Smooth and easy. Worth watching, because work that felt smooth at the time is often the work that is gone a week later.
When how sure you feel matches how right you actually are. Most people are badly calibrated after a tool has explained something to them.

teacher_notes.teacher_tip: Do not open with a warning. The single most common way this lesson fails is that pupils decide in the first ninety seconds that it is another assembly about cheating and stop listening. The 72 percent figure in the starter exists to prevent exactly that, so do not skip it or soften it.

evidence_base.claim: Cluster randomised across about fifty classes, nearly 1,000 pupils in grades 9 to 11 at one Turkish secondary school, autumn 2023. Answers arm plus 48 percent in practice and minus 17 percent on the unaided exam against control. Hints arm plus 127 percent in practice and statistically indistinguishable from control on the exam, with no positive effect observed. Honors classrooms were excluded as non randomly composed, so the analytic sample is below 1,000. Both practice figures were scored while pupils still held the tool, so they measure performance rather than learning.
evidence_base.source: Bastani, Bastani, Sungu, Ge, Kabakci and Mariman (2025), Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: evidence from high school mathematics, PNAS 122(26), e2422633122

evidence_base.claim: 72 percent of those offered an AI tool declined it. That figure is from the 704 pupil qualitative strand across 20 schools, not the 3,100 survey, and the task was a short paragraph about AI itself inside a study, so treat it as a ceiling rather than the everyday rate. 15 percent said they had been given enough guidance.
evidence_base.source: Oxford University Press (9 June 2026), Navigating AI in Education: Pupils' perspectives on the role of AI in the classroom

evidence_base.claim: 62 percent of pupils said AI had negatively affected their skills. This is a perception item rather than a measured effect, and it belongs to a different report from the 72 percent above.
evidence_base.source: Oxford University Press (15 October 2025), Teaching the AI Native Generation, n=2,000 aged 13 to 18

evidence_base.claim: 52 percent of teenagers said they were confident recognising AI generated content, and a quarter of those confident teenagers could not correctly identify the AI generated image they were shown. Ofcom's base is teenagers, so most of a Year 7 class sits below it.
evidence_base.source: Ofcom (21 May 2026), Children and Parents: Media Use and Attitudes Report 2025/26

evidence_base.claim: A computer reader is permitted, including in papers or sections of papers testing reading. A human reader is not permitted to read questions or text in a paper or section testing reading, including the reading section of GCSE English Language, where up to 50 percent extra time may be granted instead.
evidence_base.source: JCQ, Access Arrangements and Reasonable Adjustments: General and Vocational qualifications, 1 September 2025 to 31 August 2026, March 2026 amended version

evidence_base.claim: Self rated understanding on a 1 to 7 scale falls after producing a step by step causal explanation, a medium effect, Cohen's d about 0.49 as recomputed by Johnson and colleagues (2016). The effect is specific to causal and mechanistic knowledge rather than facts, procedures or narratives, which is why the classroom drill names something that works in steps.
evidence_base.source: Rozenblit and Keil (2002), The misunderstood limits of folk science: an illusion of explanatory depth, Cognitive Science 26(5), 521 to 562

evidence_base.claim: The illusion was found for devices in children in grades 2 and 4, roughly ages 7 to 10, but not in kindergarteners and not for procedures. No study covers 11 to 13 year olds, so applying it to this class is an inference between that result and the adult one.
evidence_base.source: Mills and Keil (2004), Knowing the limits of one's understanding, Journal of Experimental Child Psychology 87(1)

hard_questions.answer: Almost everything in this lesson is allowed. Your school will have a rule about what you must declare and you should follow it. This lesson is about something else: what it costs you, which is a question the rules do not answer.
hard_questions.question: So is using it cheating or not?

hard_questions.answer: No, and the exam board agrees with you by name. A reader clears something out of the way so you can get to the thinking. That is a ramp. Nothing in this lesson is aimed at you.
hard_questions.question: What if I use a reader or a laptop? Is that on the bad list?

hard_questions.answer: Then a hint is the right move, and that is not a failure. Struggling with no way in is not learning, it is just being stuck. Get in with the smallest help that works, then do the rest.
hard_questions.question: What if I genuinely cannot start without it?

hard_questions.answer: Because you will be using these tools for the next fifty years and somebody has to tell you where to stand. A ban is a rule for this room. This is a method for the rest of it.
hard_questions.question: My teachers just ban it. Why are you telling me how to use it?

misconceptions: That the lesson is about cheating. It is not. Every case in the practise set is something a pupil is allowed to do, and the question is what it costs them.
That using AI more is the problem. In the trial, the group that came out unharmed used it as much as the group that came out 17 percent down.
That a reader, a scribe or text to speech is a soft option. Those are access arrangements, the exam board permits them by name, and this lesson says so explicitly.
That struggling on your own is always better. If a pupil cannot get started at all, unaided struggle is not learning, it is just failing, and a hint is the correct move.
teacher_notes.paper_fallback: Everything runs without screens. The six practise cases are on the sheet, the sort can be done as a three column table on paper or as a stand in three corners activity, and the explain it back test needs nothing at all.
teacher_notes.commitment_stem: My commitment: the next piece of work I use AI on, the part I will do myself is...

differentiation.stretch: Case four is genuinely undecidable without more information. Ask the strongest pupils to write the two versions of the task that would flip the answer, then argue which is more likely and why.
differentiation.support: Bookmark strip with the three thinking test questions on the table throughout. Do practise cases one and two together using the stem: the task is teaching me... so this is a... Pupils may answer on the page rather than to the room at any point.

prior_knowledge: Pupils have used a chatbot for schoolwork at least once, which is true of roughly six in ten of this age group.
Pupils know what a mark scheme is and have seen one for at least one subject.

worksheet_items.text: You are dyslexic. You have a computer read the history source aloud so you can answer questions about what it says.
Maths homework on solving equations. You photograph each question and copy the worked answers.
You have written an essay. You ask a chatbot which paragraph is weakest and why, then you rewrite it yourself.
Spanish homework. You write it in English and have it translated.
You are stuck on question four and have been for ten minutes. You ask for a hint, not the answer, then carry on.
Book review on a novel you did not read. You ask for a summary and write from that.
Your own homework this week. Name it, then draw the line yourself.

parent_questions.answer: No, and we are not teaching them to avoid it either. We teach one question they run on each task: what is this piece of work actually trying to teach me? Whatever that is stays with them, and the tool can touch everything else. That is a decision they make per task rather than a rule we hand down, which is why it still works when we are not there.
parent_questions.question: Are you teaching my child to use ChatGPT for their homework?

parent_questions.answer: It would be simpler and it does not hold. Your child will use these tools for the rest of their life and nobody has shown them where to stand. A ban also pushes it out of sight, so the first time it goes wrong we are the last to hear. The trial we teach from found that the pupils who came out undamaged used AI as much as the ones who came out behind. What differed was what they asked it for.
parent_questions.question: Would it not be simpler to ban it?

parent_questions.answer: The opposite, and the lesson says so out loud in the first case the class sorts. Access arrangements are permitted by the exam board by name, and a computer reader is allowed even in a paper that tests reading. They are a ramp to the work, not a substitute for it. If your child uses one, this lesson is the reason they can stop feeling awkward about it.
parent_questions.question: My child has a reader, a scribe or text to speech. Is this lesson calling that cheating?

parent_questions.answer: The note that went home has it. Do not ask whether they understood their homework, because that feeling is unreliable and this lesson explains why. Ask them to shut the tab and explain it to you, every step. The place they go quiet is the part that was borrowed rather than learned, and the kitchen table is a much cheaper place to find it than an exam hall.
parent_questions.question: What should I do at home?

subject_knowledge.body: Memory is strengthened by effortful retrieval, so a tool that removes the effort removes the strengthening even while the visible output improves. That is why performance during practice and learning measured later can move in opposite directions, which is exactly what the Bastani trial found.
subject_knowledge.heading: The mechanism is effort transfer, not screen time

subject_knowledge.body: The second mechanism is metacognitive. Access to a tool inflates a person's estimate of their own knowledge, so pupils cannot detect the loss by introspection and need an actual test. This is why the lesson runs the explain it back drill live rather than describing it.
subject_knowledge.heading: Why they cannot feel the loss happening

subject_knowledge.body: The access versus substitution distinction is not our invention. It is the same test the regulators apply to access arrangements, that an adjustment is refused where it would change what the qualification is measuring. That is why it is both defensible and already embedded in the rules.
subject_knowledge.heading: The ramp and swap test is the regulators' own

subject_knowledge.body: Worth having straight before a pupil or a SENCO asks. A computer reader is permitted, including in papers or sections testing reading. What is barred in a section testing reading is a HUMAN reader, because a person reading aloud supplies nuance and the nuance is what is being marked. A candidate who would normally have a reader gets up to 50 percent extra time in that section instead. The bar is on sections, not whole papers.
subject_knowledge.heading: What the exam board actually says about readers

subject_knowledge.body: The maths trial was one large Turkish secondary school, pupils aged roughly 14 to 17, cluster randomised across about fifty classes. Nobody in it was the age of this class. The illusion of explanatory depth work covers ages 7 to 10 and adults, with no study on 11 to 13 year olds. Both results are borrowed from either side of this age group, which is reasonable and is still an inference. Saying that out loud models the honesty the lesson is asking for.
subject_knowledge.heading: Where we are extrapolating, and you should say so

teacher_notes.essential_question: How do I tell the difference between help that gets me to the work and help that does the work?
teacher_notes.learning_objective: To decide, for a given task, which part of the thinking must stay with me and where a tool may legitimately help.
key_learning_points: The same AI tool improved practice scores and lowered exam scores, and the only difference was whether it gave hints or answers.
The test that decides it is what the task is teaching you, not whether the tool is allowed.
Using a tool inflates how well you think you understand, so the feeling of understanding cannot be trusted as evidence.
Support should be reduced one step at a time once it has been earned, not dropped all at once.
